{{< include ../includes/generated-guided-context-en-embedding-space.qmd >}}

::: {.chapter-lead}
After tokenization, each token receives an **integer identifier** (*token ID*). The identifier does not express the token's meaning: it retrieves the **learned numerical vector** associated with that token. The model selects this vector from a matrix called the *embedding matrix*. The Transformer then processes these vectors using positional information and context to produce contextualized representations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- explain how an integer token ID acts as a row index in a learned matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$;
- distinguish an initial token embedding vector from the contextualized hidden states produced by Transformer layers;
- justify why numerical proximity of token IDs implies neither geometric nor semantic closeness in embedding space.
:::


<div class="epistemic-badges">
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-concept">Verified concept</span>
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-status">Architecture: Transformer Input</span>
</div>


::: {.callout-tip title="The one-minute mental model"}
An ID is an integer used as a **row index** (sometimes called a *row address*) in the embedding matrix: it tells the model which row to select, not where the token lies in vector space. The selected row contains the learned vector associated with the token. That vector—not the ID—can be represented as a point in embedding space. Two occurrences of the same ID retrieve the same initial vector; context is incorporated later by the Transformer.

**Key idea:** the token is a vocabulary unit, the ID identifies it, and the embedding vector is its learned numerical representation.


:::

## From token to vector: follow one example

In this lesson, $E$ denotes the **embedding matrix**: a parameter table with one row per ID. Each row is a vector of real numbers. Selecting the vector associated with an ID is called an *embedding lookup*.

Consider the English token `bank`, used in the [contextualized representations](contextualized-representations.qmd) lesson in two sentences: *The river bank eroded* and *The financial bank collapsed*. To isolate the mechanism, assume the tokenizer assigns the same ID to both occurrences. The actual ID depends on the tokenizer; the number below is fictitious.

The same lookup applies to the tokens in “What have the Romans ever done for us?”: each ID selects its row in the matrix. The sentence's content does not turn lookup into an interpretation of meaning.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["Text: « bank »"] --> B["Token: bank"]
    B --> C["Token ID: 4821 (illustrative)"]
    C --> D["Embedding lookup: select E[4821]"]
    subgraph M["Embedding matrix E: V rows × d columns"]
      R0["Row 4820: d numbers"]
      R1["Row 4821: d numbers · selected"]
      R2["Row 4822: d numbers"]
    end
    D --> R1
    R1 --> V["Initial vector x = E[4821]"]
    V --> P["Architecture-dependent positional handling"]
    P --> T["Transformer layers and context"]
    T --> H["Contextualized representation"]
```

The *lookup* does not calculate the meaning of `bank` or inspect neighboring words: it selects the initial vector associated with the ID. Both occurrences therefore have the same initial vector if they share the same ID. Their representations can differ after positional handling and the Transformer's layers.

For another visualization of the path from tokens to vectors in GPT-2, see [Jay Alammar's The Illustrated GPT-2](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-gpt2/). The diagram above is an original, simplified illustration; it does not reproduce an external figure.


## Where do the vectors come from?

A tokenizer splits text into tokens and assigns each token an **ID**. The model uses that ID to select the corresponding vector from its **embedding matrix**, denoted by $E$:

\[
E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}
\]

- $V$ is the vocabulary size: the matrix has one row per ID.
- $d$ is the embedding dimension: each row contains $d$ real numbers.
- $E[i]$ denotes the vector in the row associated with ID $i$.

This selection is called an *embedding lookup*. For example, if the token `bank` receives the fictitious ID 4821, the lookup returns $E[4821]$. The number 4821 does not describe the meaning of `bank`; it only tells the model which row to select.

### How is this matrix learned?

The matrix $E$ is part of the neural network's **parameters**. In a standard training setup, its values are initialized (often randomly) and then adjusted along with the model's other parameters. At each training step, the model predicts the next token, computes a loss from the observed target, and uses backpropagation and an optimizer to update parameters, including the relevant embedding rows.

The table is therefore neither a dictionary of definitions nor a list of hand-written coordinates: its vectors are learned from patterns in the training sequences. For the role of the [loss function](loss.qmd) and [gradients](gradients.qmd), see the dedicated lessons.

In a Transformer, this representation is then transformed by the network's layers. Three objects should be distinguished:

- **Token embedding:** the initial vector retrieved from the vocabulary matrix.
- **Contextualized representation:** a vector produced after processing context, including through attention.
- **Sentence or document embedding:** a vector computed by a model and aggregation method designed to represent a longer text.

These objects are not interchangeable. A method suited to sentence embeddings for document retrieval does not automatically transfer to a language model's internal activations.

### A historical distinction: static word vectors

Before contextual language models, methods such as Word2Vec learned **one vector per word type** from patterns in its surrounding words. CBOW predicts a target word from its context; Skip-gram predicts surrounding words from a target word. In a trained Word2Vec model, the vector for a vocabulary entry such as `bank` is the same wherever that word appears.

A Transformer starts differently: its embedding table maps each **token ID** (often a subword unit, not a whole word) to an initial vector. The same ID retrieves the same initial row, but subsequent layers combine it with positional and contextual information, so the resulting hidden state can differ across occurrences. Thus, a static Word2Vec word vector, a Transformer token embedding, and a contextualized hidden state are related ideas, but they are not interchangeable.

This is a conceptual contrast, not a claim that modern Transformer embeddings are initialized or trained like Word2Vec. See [Mikolov et al. (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) for the original word-representation architectures.

## From the principle to the calculation

Embedding lookup is simple: each ID selects its corresponding row in the table, without mixing positions or interpreting the numerical value of the ID. The micro-workbench below checks these invariants on a small NumPy example.

::: {.micro-workbench}
::: {.micro-workbench-header}
MICRO-WORKBENCH · VECTORIZED EMBEDDING LOOKUP (NUMPY)
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-body}
```python
import numpy as np

# Vocabulary matrix V=5 tokens, dimension d=2
E = np.array([
    [0.1, 0.0],   # ID 0
    [0.0, 0.2],   # ID 1
    [0.8, -0.1],  # ID 2
    [-0.2, 0.5],  # ID 3
    [0.3, 0.7],   # ID 4
], dtype=np.float64)

# Batch of 2 sequences of length L=3
token_ids = np.array([
    [2, 0, 3],  # Sequence A
    [1, 2, 4],  # Sequence B
])

# Vectorized lookup via direct NumPy integer indexing (row selection)
X = E[token_ids]

# Invariant 1: output tensor shape (B=2, L=3, d=2)
assert X.shape == (2, 3, 2)

# Invariant 2: same ID = exact same row selected in both sequences
assert np.array_equal(X[0, 0], E[2])
assert np.array_equal(X[1, 1], E[2])
assert np.array_equal(X[0, 0], X[1, 1])

# Invariant 3: consecutive IDs (2 and 3) have no geometric distance constraint
d_2_3 = float(np.linalg.norm(E[2] - E[3]))
d_0_4 = float(np.linalg.norm(E[0] - E[4]))
print(f"X shape: {X.shape}")
print(f"Distance E[2]-E[3]: {d_2_3:.3f} | Distance E[0]-E[4]: {d_0_4:.3f}")
```
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-footer}
Lookup is row selection: at each position $(b, \ell)$ of the batch, the output vector is exactly row $E[\mathrm{id}]$ of the table; two occurrences of the same token ID therefore retrieve identical initial vectors.
:::
:::

<details class="spot-the-fallacy">
<summary>Common Fallacy: “Two tokens with consecutive numerical IDs (e.g. 2 and 3) have geometrically close embedding vectors”</summary>
<div class="fallacy-content">
<p><strong>Counterexample:</strong> The integer ID is solely a <em>row address</em> in the matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$. Integer ordering is an artifact of tokenizer construction (frequency ranking, merge order in BPE, or byte values), not vector-space geometry. Adjacent rows $E_2$ and $E_3$ are $d$-dimensional vectors initialized independently and updated along different gradient trajectories. Their geometric distance shares zero relationship with the numerical difference $|3 - 2| = 1$.</p>
</div>
</details>

## From initial embeddings to contextualized representations

Lookup ends when a row is selected from the embedding matrix; it does not contextualize the vector. Positional information and processing by Transformer layers come afterwards, with mechanisms that depend on the architecture. To keep these stages distinct, see the dedicated lessons on [positional encoding](positional-encoding.qmd) and [contextualized representations](contextualized-representations.qmd).

During training, gradients can update the embedding-matrix rows used by examples. For tensor shapes and operations, see [tensors](tensors.qmd); for the preceding stages of the input chain, see [from text to tokens](text-data.qmd) and [tokenization strategies](tokenization-strategies.qmd).

## Interpreting geometry with care

![Schematic projection of an embedding space.](../images/embedding-space-en.svg){fig-alt="Points grouped in an abstract plane. The groups are illustrative; the axes do not necessarily correspond to human concepts." width=100%}

This projection is illustrative: real embeddings often have hundreds or thousands of coordinates, and a 2D representation can distort distances and neighbourhoods.

Geometric proximity depends on the model, layer, training objective, and metric. It does not prove that two texts are equivalent or that a document correctly answers a question—negation can reverse meaning even when most of the vocabulary is shared.

For a deeper treatment without conflating geometry with the lookup mechanism, see the pages on [cosine similarity](cosine-similarity.qmd) and the [linearity hypothesis for representations](embedding-linearity.qmd).
